title: Secular Buddhism
hookLine: practitioners who keep the practice and set aside rebirth and cosmology; others disagree; each explains itself

lines: KEEP THE CUSHION, SET ASIDE THE COSMOS?
cards: Can a person keep the cushion and set aside the cosmos? Sit every morning, keep the precepts, read the suttas closely, and still say, about rebirth and realms of gods and ghosts: I don't know, or I don't think so?
Some practitioners say yes, and call themselves secular Buddhists. Others, teachers rooted in old lineages, say this cuts out something the Buddha himself put at the center. Both read the same texts.
This week ends with a question, not a verdict.

teach.h: KEEP THE PRACTICE, HOLD THE COSMOS OPEN.
teach.b: First, what secular Buddhists keep and set aside. They keep meditation, the precepts, the noble truths and the eightfold path, often read as things to do, not things to believe.
They set aside, or hold open, rebirth, karma across lifetimes and the traditional map of heavens and hells.

teach.h: THE SECULAR CASE: COME AND SEE.
teach.b: The writer Stephen Batchelor is one voice among them, and secular sanghas gather in person and online. Second, their case, in their words.

They point to the Buddha's call to see for yourself, in the sutta to the Kalamas from day six fifty-seven: don't accept a teaching just because of tradition, report or a teacher's authority, but know for yourselves what leads to harm and what leads to good.
They point, too, to the old phrase ehipassiko, come and see. Practice, they say, is what can be tested in this life.
Third, the traditional reply. Teachers in Theravada, Tibetan and other lineages answer that rebirth and karma run all through the suttas.

On the night of his awakening, the texts say, the Buddha saw his own past lives and the passing away and arising of beings according to their deeds. And nibbana, in those texts, is the end of rebirth itself.
They note that the Kalama sutta goes on: the Buddha describes a person free of hatred who is at ease whether or not there is a world after this one. Both sides quote this sutta.
Fourth, the week. A courtyard of householder priests, a silent course, lay teachers in rented rooms, a circle on an altar, a new order, a new vehicle, and now this.
Each new form has had to answer the same question, what do we keep, and each explains its own answer.

how: Secular Buddhists practice meditation and the precepts and study the suttas while setting aside or holding open rebirth and traditional cosmology; teachers in traditional lineages answer that rebirth and karma are central to the Buddha's teaching, and both sides cite the Kalama Sutta.

o: Buddhist teaching kept out of public schools and government
keeping the practice, with rebirth and the old cosmos held open
meditation taught by lay teachers rather than by robed monks

p: past lives seen, in the texts

s: secular Buddhists give up meditation and ethics
they keep meditation, the precepts and the path, and set aside or hold open rebirth and cosmology.
traditional teachers say rebirth runs through the suttas
including the night of the awakening and nibbana as the end of rebirth.
only one side quotes the Kalama sutta
secular readers cite its call to know for yourself; traditional readers cite how it goes on.

games.q: at a sitting group, one friend says, 'I meditate, but I don't believe in rebirth.' another says, 'then it isn't the Buddha's path.' what does today's lesson do?
o: let each one explain their view in their own words.
games.why: each explains itself. both sides are serious, both read the same suttas, and this path ranks neither.

practice: Bring to mind a view on a big question that you don't share, and picture someone who holds it well, at their most thoughtful.

Let them explain it in your mind, in their own words, all the way to the end, without arguing back; just breathe, listen, and notice what your body does. When they finish, thank them silently and let the picture go.

wordCard.voice: Secular Buddhism. Practitioners who keep meditation and ethics and set aside rebirth and traditional cosmology, while others in the tradition disagree. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali ehipassiko, come and see: an old description of the dhamma, quoted by secular and traditional Buddhists alike.

carryVoice: Your line: each explains itself. A question held open, heard from both sides. That's the week.
